candidate_class: Chat-exposed Google Calendar event as server-side operation record

official_public_sources.finding: Underlying Calendar API events.insert allows a client-chosen event ID; Google documents this as preventing duplicate event creation after ambiguous success.
Underlying API exposes event get and delete by eventId.
Google Workspace APIs are governed by project/user quotas; daily quotas are finite and reset on a schedule.
Google announced standardized Workspace API quotas and a 2026 path where usage above standard daily thresholds can require billing and incur charges.

tested_scope.scope_guard: No Calendar event was created, updated, searched, read, or deleted; only connector schema and official public documentation were evaluated.

gate_results.duplicate_or_ambiguous_write_reconciliat: fails_without_exposed_client_supplied_event_id; free-text search is not uniqueness-enforcing and cannot prove absence of a concurrent duplicate
gate_results.finite_quota_dependency: fails_zero-quota-independence_gate_in_tested_scope because Calendar API is governed by finite project/user usage quotas
gate_results.incremental_monetary_cost: not provably zero independent of usage tier; official 2026 policy announces billing/charges above standard daily thresholds
gate_results.external_target_dependency: requires an authenticated Calendar account and would create a user-visible resource if executed

counterexample: The underlying Calendar API is unusually close to the desired primitive because a client-supplied event ID can prevent duplicate creation and events can be read/deleted by ID. However, the current Chat create_event connector does not expose the event ID field at all. It therefore cannot precommit a caller-controlled server key before an ambiguous create, and a lost create response cannot be deterministically reconciled by direct ID lookup. Searching by title/description cannot supply server-enforced uniqueness and can race into duplicates. In addition, Calendar API operation depends on finite Workspace API quotas and current official policy does not establish quota-independent zero-cost use at arbitrary sustained load.
